LIVE TESTIMONY AT FAMILY LAW HEARINGS (FAMILY CODE SECTION 217; ELKINS V. SUPERIOR COURT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Dana Aoki Whitfield · Marcus Ellery Whitfield

PARTIES, SCOPE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Live Testimony Information Sheet concerns Dana Aoki Whitfield and Marcus Ellery Whitfield in connection with the request for order on child support set for hearing, a matter pending or to be filed in the California superior court for Alameda County. It surveys what California law says about when a family court must receive live testimony at a hearing: the text of Family Code section 217, the bill that added it, the general procedural rule of Family Code section 210, the California Supreme Court decision that prompted the statute (Elkins v. Superior Court (2007) 41 Cal.4th 1337), the rule of court the statute directed the Judicial Council to adopt (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.113), and two published Court of Appeal decisions construing section 217 (In re Marriage of Swain (2018) 21 Cal.App.5th 830 and In re Marriage of George & Deamon (2019) 35 Cal.App.5th 476). It states what those authorities say and hold. It does not determine whether live testimony is required at any hearing in this matter, whether good cause to refuse live testimony exists, whether any objection has been preserved or forfeited, or what any party should do; those are matters for the court, or for the parties' own stipulation.

THE STATUTE: FAMILY CODE SECTION 217 AND ITS THREE SUBDIVISIONS
Family Code section 217 governs the receipt of live testimony at family law hearings. Subdivision (a) states that at a hearing on any order to show cause or notice of motion brought pursuant to the Family Code, absent a stipulation of the parties or a finding of good cause under subdivision (b), the court shall receive any live, competent testimony that is relevant and within the scope of the hearing, and that the court may ask questions of the parties. Subdivision (b) permits a court in appropriate cases to make a finding of good cause to refuse to receive live testimony, requires the court to state its reasons for that finding on the record or in writing, and directed the Judicial Council to adopt, by January 1, 2012, a statewide rule of court on the factors bearing on good cause. Subdivision (c) requires a party seeking to present live testimony from witnesses other than the parties to file and serve a witness list, with a brief description of the anticipated testimony, before the hearing, and provides that if the list is not served the court may on request grant a brief continuance and make appropriate temporary orders. The section was added by Statutes 2010, chapter 352, section 3 (Assembly Bill 939), effective January 1, 2011.

HOW THE LEGISLATURE DESCRIBED THE BILL THAT ADDED SECTION 217 -- AND HOW IT DIFFERS FROM THE ENACTED TEXT
Assembly Bill 939 (2009-2010 Reg. Sess.), chaptered as Statutes 2010, chapter 352, was a committee bill making several changes to family law procedure, of which section 217 was one. The Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the change as requiring the court in a family law action to receive all live, competent, and relevant testimony at a hearing of an order to show cause or notice of motion, unless the parties stipulate otherwise or the court makes a finding of good cause to refuse to hear the testimony. A published Court of Appeal decision has quoted that Digest language when construing the section.

THE BACKGROUND RULE: CIVIL PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE APPLY IN FAMILY LAW PROCEEDINGS
Family Code section 210 supplies the general procedural baseline for proceedings under the Family Code. Except to the extent that another statute or a rule adopted by the Judicial Council provides applicable rules, the rules of practice and procedure applicable to civil actions generally -- including the vexatious litigant provisions of Code of Civil Procedure title 3a, beginning with section 391 -- apply to and constitute the rules of practice and procedure in Family Code proceedings. The California Supreme Court relied on this section when it held that an individual superior court could not adopt a hearsay exception applicable only to marital dissolution trials.

ELKINS V. SUPERIOR COURT (2007): DECLARATIONS ARE HEARSAY AND CANNOT SUBSTITUTE FOR TESTIMONY AT A CONTESTED DISSOLUTION TRIAL
Elkins v. Superior Court arose from a Contra Costa County local rule and trial scheduling order requiring parties to present their cases at dissolution trials by written declaration, with direct examination allowed only in unusual circumstances. The California Supreme Court resolved the case on statutory rather than constitutional grounds, stating that it need not reach the petitioner's constitutional claim because, as applied to contested marital dissolution trials, the rule and order were inconsistent with various statutory provisions, and explaining that under state law marital dissolution trials proceed under the same general rules of procedure that govern other civil trials. The court stated that declarations constitute hearsay and are inadmissible at trial subject to specific statutory exceptions, unless the parties stipulate to their admission or fail to object; that Code of Civil Procedure section 2009, which permits affidavits in certain motion matters, does not authorize their admission at a contested trial leading to judgment; and it concluded that the local rule and order were inconsistent with the hearsay rule to the extent they rendered written declarations admissible as a basis for decision in a contested marital dissolution trial.

THE DISTINCTION ELKINS DREW BETWEEN TRIALS AND POSTJUDGMENT MOTIONS
The Elkins opinion did not treat every family law proceeding alike. Responding to an argument that the line between hearings on motions and trials is illusory in dissolution practice, the court stated that it had drawn a distinction between hearings at which a judgment is entered and hearings on postjudgment motions, noting that a postjudgment motion to modify a final custody order requires a showing of significantly changed circumstances and that a presumption of correctness attaches to the judgment. Because Elkins was decided in 2007 and section 217 was added in 2010, later decisions have had to consider what the statute did to that distinction; those decisions are addressed in the clauses on In re Marriage of Swain and In re Marriage of George & Deamon below.

THE PASSAGE THAT NAMED A TASK FORCE -- AND A MISQUOTATION OF IT IN THE TASK FORCE'S OWN REPORT
Elkins closed with a policy discussion that became the charter for the statutory change. The court said that in light of the volume of cases faced by trial courts it understood their efforts to streamline family law procedures, but that family law litigants should not be subjected to second-class status or deprived of access to justice, and that the same judicial resources and safeguards should be committed to a family law trial as are committed to other civil proceedings. In a footnote the court recommended that the Judicial Council establish a task force to study and propose measures to assist trial courts in achieving efficiency and fairness in marital dissolution proceedings and to ensure access to justice for litigants, many of whom are self-represented. The Judicial Council appointed the Elkins Family Law Task Force, whose April 2010 final report opens with that passage; Assembly Bill 939 followed.

CALIFORNIA RULES OF COURT, RULE 5.113: PURPOSE AND THE SIX GOOD-CAUSE FACTORS
Section 217(b) directed the Judicial Council to adopt a rule on the factors bearing on good cause; rule 5.113 of the California Rules of Court, adopted effective January 1, 2013, is that rule. Subdivision (a) states that under Family Code section 217, at a hearing on any request for order brought under the Family Code, absent a stipulation of the parties or a finding of good cause under (b), the court must receive any live, competent, and admissible testimony that is relevant and within the scope of the hearing. Subdivision (b) lists six factors a court must consider, in addition to the rules of evidence, in making a good-cause finding to refuse live testimony: whether a substantive matter is at issue; whether material facts are in controversy; whether live testimony is necessary to assess credibility; the right of the parties to question anyone submitting reports or other information to the court; whether a party offering nonparty testimony has complied with section 217(c); and any other factor that is just and equitable.

RULE 5.113 CONTINUED: STATING REASONS, CHILDREN'S TESTIMONY, WITNESS LISTS, CONTINUANCES, AND QUESTIONS FROM THE BENCH
The remaining subdivisions of rule 5.113 address what follows a good-cause finding and how testimony is arranged. Subdivision (c) requires a court that finds good cause to exclude live testimony to state its reasons on the record or in writing, and states that the court need state only those factors on which the finding is based. Subdivision (d) provides that when receiving or excluding testimony from minor children the court must, in addition to satisfying Evidence Code section 765, follow the procedures in Family Code section 3042 and rule 5.250. Subdivision (e) requires that witness lists under section 217(c) be served with the request for order or responsive papers, notes that Judicial Council form FL-321 may be used, and states that if no witness list has been served the court may require an offer of proof before allowing a nonparty witness to testify. Subdivision (f) directs the court to consider whether a brief continuance is needed so a litigant can prepare to question another party's witness. Subdivision (g) provides that whenever the court receives live testimony it may elicit testimony by directing questions to the parties and other witnesses.

IN RE MARRIAGE OF SWAIN (2018): A DECLARATION THE OBJECTING PARTY COULD NOT CROSS-EXAMINE
In re Marriage of Swain involved a postjudgment motion to terminate spousal support. The supported spouse filed an income and expense declaration but did not serve it and did not appear; the paying spouse objected that he could not cross-examine her about it, and the trial court nonetheless relied on the declaration in its ruling. The Court of Appeal reviewed the interpretation of section 217 de novo, described the history of the section and the case law preceding it as reflecting a concern for the value of live testimony rather than deciding substantive motions on competing declarations, and held that section 217, read with that history, precludes reliance on inadmissible hearsay over a party's objection -- subject to the good-cause provision of subdivision (b) -- at least where the party has no opportunity for cross-examination. The court stated that under section 217, absent a stipulation or a good cause finding, the objecting party had a right to any live testimony that was relevant and within the scope of the hearing, that such testimony included the opportunity to cross-examine the declarant, and that the proper remedy for the absence of that opportunity was to exclude the written declaration from evidence.

Family Code section 217 governs the receipt of live testimony at family law hearings. Subdivision (a) states that at a hearing on any order to show cause or notice of motion brought pursuant to the Family Code, absent a stipulation of the parties or a finding of good cause under subdivision (b), the court shall receive any live, competent testimony that is relevant and within the scope of the hearing, and that the court may ask questions of the parties. Subdivision (b) permits a court in appropriate cases to make a finding of good cause to refuse to receive live testimony, requires the court to state its reasons for that finding on the record or in writing, and directed the Judicial Council to adopt, by January 1, 2012, a statewide rule of court on the factors bearing on good cause. Subdivision (c) requires a party seeking to present live testimony from witnesses other than the parties to file and serve a witness list, with a brief description of the anticipated testimony, before the hearing, and provides that if the list is not served the court may on request grant a brief continuance and make appropriate temporary orders. The section was added by Statutes 2010, chapter 352, section 3 (Assembly Bill 939), effective January 1, 2011.

expectedJSON.body: Section 217(b) directed the Judicial Council to adopt a rule on the factors bearing on good cause; rule 5.113 of the California Rules of Court, adopted effective January 1, 2013, is that rule. Subdivision (a) states that under Family Code section 217, at a hearing on any request for order brought under the Family Code, absent a stipulation of the parties or a finding of good cause under (b), the court must receive any live, competent, and admissible testimony that is relevant and within the scope of the hearing. Subdivision (b) lists six factors a court must consider, in addition to the rules of evidence, in making a good-cause finding to refuse live testimony: whether a substantive matter is at issue; whether material facts are in controversy; whether live testimony is necessary to assess credibility; the right of the parties to question anyone submitting reports or other information to the court; whether a party offering nonparty testimony has complied with section 217(c); and any other factor that is just and equitable.

expectedJSON.body: The remaining subdivisions of rule 5.113 address what follows a good-cause finding and how testimony is arranged. Subdivision (c) requires a court that finds good cause to exclude live testimony to state its reasons on the record or in writing, and states that the court need state only those factors on which the finding is based. Subdivision (d) provides that when receiving or excluding testimony from minor children the court must, in addition to satisfying Evidence Code section 765, follow the procedures in Family Code section 3042 and rule 5.250. Subdivision (e) requires that witness lists under section 217(c) be served with the request for order or responsive papers, notes that Judicial Council form FL-321 may be used, and states that if no witness list has been served the court may require an offer of proof before allowing a nonparty witness to testify. Subdivision (f) directs the court to consider whether a brief continuance is needed so a litigant can prepare to question another party's witness. Subdivision (g) provides that whenever the court receives live testimony it may elicit testimony by directing questions to the parties and other witnesses.

expectedJSON.body: In re Marriage of Swain involved a postjudgment motion to terminate spousal support. The supported spouse filed an income and expense declaration but did not serve it and did not appear; the paying spouse objected that he could not cross-examine her about it, and the trial court nonetheless relied on the declaration in its ruling. The Court of Appeal reviewed the interpretation of section 217 de novo, described the history of the section and the case law preceding it as reflecting a concern for the value of live testimony rather than deciding substantive motions on competing declarations, and held that section 217, read with that history, precludes reliance on inadmissible hearsay over a party's objection -- subject to the good-cause provision of subdivision (b) -- at least where the party has no opportunity for cross-examination. The court stated that under section 217, absent a stipulation or a good cause finding, the objecting party had a right to any live testimony that was relevant and within the scope of the hearing, that such testimony included the opportunity to cross-examine the declarant, and that the proper remedy for the absence of that opportunity was to exclude the written declaration from evidence.

citations.quote: We agree that section 217, when considered in light of its legislative history and the case law leading to its adoption, precludes reliance on inadmissible hearsay over a party's objection (subject to the good cause provision of section 217, subdivision (b)), at least where the party has no opportunity for cross-examination.

citations.quote: The history of section 217 and the case law that preceded it reflect a concern for the value of live testimony rather than deciding substantive motions based upon competing declarations.

citations.cite: at p. 842 (the remedy)
citations.quote: Such live testimony included the opportunity to cross-examine Sandra concerning statements in her Declaration on which the trial court might rely. The proper remedy for the absence of an opportunity for cross-examination was to exclude her written declaration from evidence.

expectedJSON.body: Swain was careful about the reach of its holding. The court stated that it need not answer the general question whether section 217 makes written declarations submitted with family law motions subject to the hearsay rule in every case, and concluded only that, at a minimum, the Code of Civil Procedure section 2009 hearsay exception does not apply to a motion to modify a family law judgment where the opposing party seeks to exclude the declaration on the ground that he or she cannot cross-examine the declarant. Surveying earlier decisions -- including Chalmers v. Hirschkop (2013) and In re Marriage of Shimkus (2016) -- the court said that none of the published cases interpreting section 217 has squarely decided that section 217 completely abrogated the hearsay exception in Code of Civil Procedure section 2009 for substantive family law motions.

No California Supreme Court decision construes section 217, and this research did not attempt to survey every Court of Appeal decision citing the section after 2019, so the statement that the question remains open is a report of what these two opinions say, not an independent survey. expectedJSON.body: In re Marriage of George & Deamon concerned a Family Code section 271 sanctions motion decided on declarations where the opposing party lived in Japan and did not appear. The Court of Appeal agreed to a point with the objecting party's reading of section 217, stating that as the plain language of the section makes clear, had she followed the proper procedures to present live competent testimony within the scope of the hearing she would have had a right to do so unless the family court found good cause to exclude it. The court held, however, that a party's personal appearance is not required, that a party who wants to examine an absent opposing party must serve a notice to appear under Code of Civil Procedure section 1987(b), and that in the context of section 217 the right to live testimony may be forfeited -- which it found had happened because no live witness was produced whose testimony the court could receive. The court also stated that nothing in section 217 requires a party to offer evidence at a motion hearing when the motion is decided solely on written submissions because no party has taken proper steps to present live testimony.

expectedJSON.body: George & Deamon also addressed what a court must do when it declines live testimony. The court acknowledged that it was not clear from the objecting party's comments that she was invoking a right to call and cross-examine the other party, and stated that had the family court judge understood her comments as a request to present live testimony from the other party, the court would have been required to make a finding of good cause to refuse to receive that testimony, which it did not do. The court concluded that the absence of an express good-cause finding was not prejudicial on these facts, reasoning in part that the court is required to receive live testimony under section 217 only if the testimony is relevant and within the scope of the hearing, and it concluded that although in certain circumstances the family court is required by section 217 to receive live testimony when deciding a motion, the family court in that case did not prejudicially err by deciding the sanctions motion on the declarations and documentary evidence alone.
